summary: A document submitted to the IETF IPng area in response to RFC 1550, discussing hosts that have many addresses. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC argues that address planning should allow a host to have more than one IP address. It describes possible uses for separate addresses and recommends leaving room for additional addresses per host.

questions: why would a host need many ip addresses
can a computer have multiple addresses
why might a host need multiple ip addresses
subtitle: A discussion of reasons a host might need multiple IP addresses.

tldr.problem: The memo questions whether counting hosts is enough for address-space planning if a host may need multiple addresses for different purposes.
tldr.mechanism: It discusses using separate addresses for services, billing policies, users, limited mobility, and hosts connected to more than one logical network.
tldr.outcome: The author recommends allowing 2^6 to 2^8 extra addresses per host to leave room for the proposed uses.

today: RFC 1681 is Informational and presents ideas for using multiple IP addresses per host. It does not specify an Internet standard.

sections.title: Why a Host Might Need More Addresses
sections.content: The author notes that most hosts have one address, but says this assumption may be wrong for future address-space planning. The memo discusses multiple addresses as one plausible way to support several goals, without claiming it is the only or best approach.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC asks planners to consider that one host may need several IP addresses. It presents multiple addressing as an idea worth considering, not as the only solution.

sections.title: Services, Billing, and User Identity
sections.content:
A separate address could identify a service on a host, allowing different services or views to use different access policies. The memo also discusses encoding charging policies in addresses and assigning a separate address to each user session for accounting or finer-grained protection.

It notes that address-based policies can avoid some reliance on name service, but also discusses risks and operational tradeoffs in the examples.
sections.plainLanguage: Different addresses could help a host separate services, identify who pays, or distinguish users. The memo presents these as possible designs with tradeoffs.

sections.title: Address Movement and Multiple Networks
sections.content: The memo describes limited mobility within a subnet: a service could move to a peer machine while keeping addresses that clients already know. It also discusses assigning addresses from more than one logical network to hosts that need to operate on both networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Addresses could move between machines to keep a service reachable, or let one host belong to two logical networks at once.

sections.title: Planning for Extra Addresses
sections.content:
The author says most proposed uses need only a handful of distinct service addresses, while addresses per user could require more. Address-mask policies and room for subnet growth also affect how much address space must be reserved.

The recommendation is to allow 2^6, and perhaps as many as 2^8, extra addresses per host.
sections.plainLanguage: The author recommends reserving extra address capacity for each host. The suggested range is 2^6 to 2^8 additional addresses.
